catalog_quote: 2.3 Tones Moro seems to have a reduced tonal system compared with neighbouring related languages. It has three phonetic tone heights, but the majority of words can be analysed as having a simple high-low contrast. This suggests that the third tone has become a downstep. Rising and falling tones are contrastive but rare. new_statements.rule_in_words: Lemoro is described purely as a tone language: two underlying level tones (H, L) with a downstepped H surfacing as a third (mid) height, plus rare contrastive rising and falling contours; tone is lexically contrastive and also marks perfective aspect and verb plurality. The description contains no statement of any kind about word stress or accentual prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: None concerning stress. (Tonal notes only: noun prefixes are always Low; mid tone typically follows a L-H sequence and is analysed as downstep; one H-M word recorded.)
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on citation forms of words; no word- or phrase-level stress discussed. Source is a 22-page circulation draft based on 2024-2025 elicitation sessions in Jos.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench & Terna 2025 describe LeMoro/LiMoro (autonym Èmóró, people Ànámōrō), headquarters Bakin Kogi (Kàzóŋgó), Bassa LGA, Plateau State, with villages in Bauchi, Kaduna and Kano States = Glottolog lemo1242 Lemoro, ISO ldj (East Kainji, Shammɔ / Lemoro-Sanga subgroup). Not to be confused with the Kordofanian Moro of Sudan (moro1285). Blench uses 'Moro' and 'LeMoro' interchangeably in the text.

sources.note: Nothing. Ch. 2 Phonology = 2.1 Consonants, 2.2 Vowels (long vowels vs VV sequences distinguished by tone behaviour), 2.3 Tones (three phonetic heights analysed as H/L plus downstep; contrastive but rare rising and falling tones; minimal sets). The words 'stress'/'accent' (prominence sense) do not occur anywhere in the 22-page text; tone also carries perfective marking and plural-verb polarity.
